description:
We are a team of third-semester undergraduate Computer Science students from NUST Balochistan Campus (NBC). 

In our Hackathon Project, we are building an interactive Space Mission Design Game that models real-world engineering trade-offs, balancing spacecraft payload, orbital mechanics, budgets, and multi-player resource management. Our goal is to create an engaging, technically grounded simulation that turns complex aerospace systems into intuitive gameplay, delivering a playable prototype
summary:
Mission Architect is an interactive web game where players design, launch and fly a complete space mission. They choose one of four missions (Earth climate, Moon ice, Mars relay or hurricane watch) and a difficulty, then work through five steps: plan the orbit and rocket, pick science instruments, build the power system, choose an antenna and launch. Players can go solo or in teams of up to four, with each player owning a phase.

It addresses the challenge by making trade-offs visible. Live meters for budget, mass, power, battery, data and survival change with every choice. A simulated flight adds random events and failures, and a report scores the mission and explains why it succeeded or failed. Players can save and compare designs and share them with other teams.

It matters because space engineering is usually taught as separate topics. Here, learners see a mission as one connected system. A friendly astronaut guide, a dictionary and “why” notes keep it approachable for newcomers, and failure is a safe way to learn.
details:
What it does and how it works
Mission Architect is a browser game where players design and fly a space mission. They pick a mission (Climate Watch, Lunar Ice Hunter, Red Planet Relay or Storm Chaser), a difficulty, and solo or team play. Then they design in four phases: orbit, rocket and lifetime, science instruments, power system, computer and spare parts, and antenna. Live meters track budget, launch mass, power, battery, data return, survival and science forecast. When the player launches, the game simulates the flight year by year, with random events and failures. The player then gets a score out of 100, a post-mission analysis explaining what went wrong, stars, badges, a postcard from their spacecraft, and a short space quiz.

Benefits

  • Teaches real mission trade-offs (mass, power, data, cost) by playing instead of reading.
  • Beginner-friendly, with a guide character (Cosmo), hints, a Space Dictionary and simple instrument names.
  • Many designs can win, so players are encouraged to experiment.
  • Free, with no install or account, and it works on phones and computers.

Intended impact

  • Spark interest in space and STEM, especially in students.
  • Build systems thinking, since every choice affects another.
  • Show that missions are built by teams, with roles for planner, scientist, engineer and comms/finance.
  • Give teachers a free classroom activity with team play and design codes to share.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks.
  • Inline SVG graphics and CSS animations for the spacecraft, astronaut and launch scene.
  • Web Audio API for sound effects, localStorage for saves, progress and the leaderboard, and the Clipboard API with base64 for shareable design codes.
  • Google Fonts (Fredoka).
  • No special hardware is needed, only a browser. (Add your own tools here, such as editors, GitHub or design software.)

Creativity

  • Engineering constraints become a game: more instruments mean more data than the antenna can send home.
  • Cosmo reacts to the player’s choices.
  • Random events and a detailed debrief teach why real teams keep margins.
  • Rewards include stars, badges, a daily challenge, a leaderboard and a shareable postcard.
  • The cosmic visual style is playful.

Factors considered

  • Realism vs. simplicity: real concepts (eclipse, radiation, distance, power loss over time) are simplified for beginners.
  • Audience: plain language, a dictionary and a Guided Mode for young or new learners.
  • Balance: different missions favor different orbits and instruments, so there’s no single best design.
  • Teamwork: roles and turn-taking for classroom use.
  • Accessibility: responsive layout, light and dark modes, a mute button and keyboard-friendly controls.
  • Technical simplicity: a single lightweight file with no server.
dataRefs: NASA State-of-the-Art Small Spacecraft Technology Report (Small Spacecraft Systems Virtual Institute)
